 City of Durham Could Revisit Minimum Wage Increases for Employees 
 Increases at the bottom of the pay scale—which are tied to Durham’s rising housing costs under the city’s livable wage ordinance—are outpacing other wages and straining the budget. 
 by 
 Justin Laidlaw and Tori Newby 
 November 18, 2026 November 18, 2026

 As Durham city staff embark on the next budget season, a familiar challenge is causing concerns for city leadership. Increases in the city’s minimum employee pay are straining its budget and causing too little differentiation between workers’ wages, prompting city officials to consider pausing next year’s planned minimum wage increase and changing its compensation structure.
 Base compensation for most city of Durham employees is calculated through a formula spelled out in the Durham Minimum Livable Wage (DMLW) ordinance. The formula is tied to market rents established by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and is averaged over four years assuming tenants are spending 30% of their income on housing.
 Since the living wage ordinance was adopted in 2019, housing costs in Durham have swelled, raising the city’s minimum pay exponentially and putting pressure on the city’s budget year-after-year. In the past three years, the city’s minimum wage jumped from $18.46 an hour in fiscal year 2024 to $25.09 in this year’s budget , a 35.9% increase. The projected rate for the upcoming fiscal year would be $27 an hour, a 7% increase from the current rate. A typical annual pay increase is only a few percentage points, according to a presentation the City Council received on Monday. 
 Increasing the wage floor would further accentuate an issue called compression, which occurs when there is little difference in wages between an organization’s lowest-paid workers and more experienced or senior staff. Ferguson said that fixing compression in the long term—by raising wages at the higher end of the pay plan—would be expensive. This year’s budget included an additional $8.4 million to help alleviate recent wage compression .

 On Monday, the Durham City Council received a presentation from Gallagher, a consulting firm the city hired to conduct a compensation study, with recommendations on how to address the compression issue and rein in annual jumps in the minimum wage while continuing to offer city of Durham employees market-competitive salaries. 
 Those recommendations include freezing the current minimum wage next fiscal year while the city revisits its compensation plans. This would keep the city’s minimum wage at $25.09 an hour for another year rather than implementing the planned increase to $27 an hour.
 Alternatively, the council could consider amending the DMLW ordinance to allow more flexibility in how the city’s minimum wage is calculated beginning next fiscal year. Durham City Manager Bo Ferguson said that the current ordinance methodology is too dependent on rent and “does not consider any other of the typical basket of economic factors that most affordability measures use.”
 In addition to pausing or amending the minimum wage ordinance, the city council could consider adjusting its pay schedule. Currently, the city uses a step plan to guide annual raises for employees. A step plan puts each staff position on a set schedule for pay increases, providing both the city and its employees with a predictable amount of money to account for each year.
 The consulting firm shared two alternative methods: an open range plan and a hybrid plan. The open range plan would do away with the current step plan and instead set any pay within a certain range based on the position and years of employment, with flexibility to reward performance and respond to market conditions. The hybrid plan is a combination of the open range and step plans; employees are on a set pay schedule until they reach a midpoint in the pay range, after which they move into an open range plan. The hybrid model received a positive response from multiple council members.
 Freezing or changing the city’s minimum wage for a year wouldn’t necessarily lock employees making that amount into their current pay rate; employees would still be able to advance through the city’s pay steps as they’re eligible.

 Ferguson said Monday that while no formal decisions have been made, he suggests keeping the current pay plan for next year’s budget, while also setting aside additional funding to make adjustments based on the recommendations from the compensation study, which is slated to finish in June. The city’s new fiscal year begins on July 1, so pay adjustments based on the study could come after the budget has already passed.
 “Obviously, we want the richest plan that we can provide to our employees while also being able to pay for it,” Ferguson said.
 The city’s wage floor has already risen faster than the rest of the wage plan for higher-level employees over the past five years, Ferguson said, and pausing the DMLW one year for most entry-level jobs would still mean all workers are getting paid a livable wage that “far outpaces” partner governments; Durham County’s minimum wage is $19.22, while minimum pay for classified workers at Durham Public Schools starts at $18.22. But Ferguson said he sees a “real harm” to employees in implementing the minimum wage increase planned for next year because of the wage compression it would cause.
 “If we do not pause the DMLW or recalculate the DMLW … we will essentially obliterate the lower half of almost all of our step plans,” Ferguson said. “And what happens, and what you saw happened last year and what we heard from a number of our employees—that is very frustrating for them as it creates a great deal of compression.”
 Durham City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg said there isn’t language in the existing ordinance that allows for a “pause” to the wage floor; the council would have to amend the ordinance. She recommended incorporating a requirement in which the council would adopt a resolution each year to outline the methodology for determining the living wage to give future councils flexibility in how it is calculated.
 Council members were wary of the attorney’s proposal. City Councilmember Shanetta Burris worried that revisiting the ordinance each year could allow too much variability, and push the council away from the original objective of providing a wage for employees that closely matches rises in cost of living.
 “I have trust issues in this moment, of trusting council every year to do a resolution around the ordinance, and ideologies may change,” Burris said. “And so we may creep away from what our goal is very soon because you have an election next year.”
 Mayor Leonardo Williams shared the city manager’s concerns about wage compression and said he would like to see a draft methodology for calculating the city’s livable wage that includes other factors besides housing costs.
 “Housing markets crash. It is actually maybe not to the benefit of workers to tie it to one piece and one piece only, and that’s where I think methodology is important,” Williams said. 
 Councilmember Carl Rist said he’d feel more comfortable slowing the increase of the wage floor, rather than pausing it altogether.
 “Our living wage ordinance is a huge asset for this community, a huge win that we’ve had,” Rist said. “The fact that we’re paying our folks a living wage like we are—a huge win, so I’m very cautious to sort of start chipping away at that one.”
 City staff will come back to the city council in the coming months with options regarding maintaining the livable wage, calculating it in a different way, and proposing an interim minimum wage for this year.
